context.hint: A cached recursive permission resolver is outermost in the resolver chain, so a cache hit returns before the inner visited-path cycle guard runs. The cache key covers tuple identity, store, model, contextual tuples and request context but not the visited-path set. The immediate uncertainty is whether a response whose metadata reports a detected cycle is inserted and replayed at all; a counting delegate and two identical subproblem calls can answer that without a full server.
context.surface: Go authorization service with a recursive check resolver, an optional in-memory check-query cache, a visited-path cycle guard, and Check plus object-listing APIs over disposable in-process servers.
assumptions: The analyst may read and edit a local source snapshot and build it with a local Go toolchain.
The cache can be enabled or disabled independently on two disposable local servers.
Tuple data is attacker-influenced but the authorization model is fixed by the service owner.
Only loopback traffic and local fixtures are used; no public deployment is contacted.
Patch mode: the deliverable is a minimal source repair plus local regression evidence and a host-side official-evaluation handoff.

incumbent.text: Skip cache insertion when the resolved subproblem response carries a cycle marker, then compare cache-enabled and cache-disabled results on a cyclic traversal and verify that ordinary acyclic subproblems still hit.

candidates.text: Skip cache insertion when the delegate's response reports a detected cycle, leaving ordinary responses cacheable. Prerequisites: cycle state is exposed in response metadata and a missing entry is safe to recompute. Bounded test: call the cache resolver twice with one delegate that returns an allowed:false, cycle-marked response and count delegate invocations; then repeat with an allowed:true response. Expected result: the cycle response is not cached (two calls) while the acyclic response is cached (one call); falsifier: either case violates the expected count or changes the returned decision. Cleanup: remove the guard.

Gate cache lookup on visited-path membership so a tuple already on the current traversal path returns a cycle denial before any cached value is read. Prerequisites: the wrapper has the same tuple-key normalization as the inner guard. Bounded test: seed a cache entry through one path, then evaluate the same tuple while it is already visited and assert the delegate is not consulted. Expected result: no stale replay; falsifier: a legitimate non-cycle recursive request loses its hit or returns a different decision. Cleanup: remove the lookup gate.

Include a canonical digest of the visited-path set in the cache key so each traversal context gets a distinct entry. Prerequisites: deterministic tuple ordering and a bounded fingerprint. Bounded test: build two requests with identical tuple/store/model/context but different visited sets, compare keys, then repeat a cyclic workload and count distinct keys. Expected result: keys differ and the wrong-path hit disappears; falsifier: unbounded key growth or unchanged keys. Cleanup: revert the key construction.

Shorten the cache TTL so path-dependent entries expire before reuse. Prerequisites: a configurable clock or short interval and toleration of a stale window. Bounded test: populate a cycle-marked entry, advance time past the TTL, and re-evaluate the tuple. Expected result: the entry is gone; falsifier: a wrong decision is still served within the TTL. Limitation: probabilistic mitigation, not a correctness guard. Cleanup: restore the original TTL.

evaluations.rationale: Initial overall plan retained as the incumbent; it proposes the direct insertion guard that the trajectory later tests.
Selected: smallest testable repair tied directly to the suspected cache insertion behavior, with a counting-delegate falsifier.
Deferred: plausible and compatible with the incumbent, but the observed uncertainty is insertion, so lookup gating is tested later.
Deferred: sound but more invasive; key cardinality and canonicalization need measurement first.
Deferred: short TTL only narrows the stale window and introduces timing flakiness.

observation.summary: A counting delegate returned an allowed:false response with a cycle marker. Two identical cache-resolver calls produced two identical responses but only one delegate invocation, proving that the cycle-marked answer was inserted and replayed. The acyclic control in the same probe was not yet run; the result establishes the insertion behavior, not an end-to-end authorization change.
observation.next_hint: Construct an end-to-end cyclic fixture where a cycle-marked subanswer is cached during one traversal and the same tuple is later queried as a root, then compare a cache-enabled server with a cache-disabled server.
